a74.speaker: Jean Codo, legislative candidate for the Alliance Force dans l'Unité (AFU) list
a74.speech: Petitions the Constitutional Court to invalidate the election of Bako Arifari Nassirou and Issa Salifou in Benin's first electoral constituency (April 30, 2011 legislative elections) due to massive, premeditated electoral fraud, including: falsified electoral rolls; pre-stamped ballots; voting by people not on any electoral roll; vote-buying and campaigning on election day; party posters displayed inside polling stations; absent or inadequate voting booths that failed to guarantee ballot secrecy; votes cast under pressure and influence; transfer, transport and trafficking of voters; and massive voting by minors and foreigners. Argues these irregularities, documented by bailiff Maître Bertrand Togla, decisively affected the outcome and that his own list would otherwise have won a seat. Separately argues that Bako Arifari Nassirou is ineligible because he simultaneously served as General Supervisor of the Political Supervisory Commission of the computerized Permanent Electoral Roll (CPS-LEPI) while running as a candidate, a conflict of interest under Article 11 of Law No. 2010-35, and used that position to certify false lists and campaign inside polling stations on election day. Concludes by asking the Court to invalidate both candidates' elections and declare himself elected.

a74.speaker: Abibou (Abidou) Djolo, USAID election observer
a74.speech: "This morning at polling station TTBV 23, Mr. Nassirou BAKO ARIFARI brought a list of fifty (50) people whose names do not appear on any electoral roll of the first constituency. They came to vote easily on the basis of a fictitious list without CENA's signature. After noting the irregularity, I went to CENA to find out more. Now, Madame Assiaka AZIA BAKO is presenting me with a similar list with a significant number of people who are supposed to vote by transfer; I firmly objected to this, and that is what caused Madame Assiaka AZIA to grab me by the collar before tearing my entire shirt."

a74.speaker: Maître Bertrand Togla, bailiff (huissier de justice), official records
a74.speech: Official records (procès-verbaux) documenting irregularities across multiple polling stations on election day, including: a man directing others to "put the stamp in the third box and join me at headquarters"; a candidate's vehicle turning away without identifying its occupant; unattended or improvised voting booths that did not guarantee ballot secrecy; a truck transporting voters between polling stations; campaign posters displayed at or near polling stations; and several minors (aged roughly 10-12) found holding and using voter cards to vote.

a74.speaker: Unnamed truck driver, Saka polling station (anonymous)
a74.speech: "I wanted to vote earlier at polling station No. 4, but the officials at that polling station found that my name does not appear on the electoral roll, so I could not vote. They also reproached me for having many people aboard my vehicle." ; "I don't know you, so by what right are you asking me to show you my voter card."

a74.speaker: Inouai Yaya, truck driver
a74.speech: "I'm coming from the Nigeria border for my boss Saley Salifou, Malanville."

a160.speaker: 125 UK Members of Parliament (cross-party letter to PM Keir Starmer)
a160.speech: They write: "British recognition of Palestine would be particularly powerful given its role as the author of the Balfour Declaration and the former Mandatory Power in Palestine. Since 1980 we have backed a two-state solution. Such a recognition would give that position substance as well as living up to a historic responsibility we have to the people under that Mandate."

a160.speaker: Sky News
a160.speech: According to Sky News, 125 MPs have signed a mass cross-party letter urging Prime Minister Keir Starmer to recognise Palestinian statehood.

a160.speaker: Emmanuel Macron, President of France (post on his official X handle)
a160.speech: "Consistent with its historic commitment to a just and lasting peace in the Middle East, I have decided that France will recognise the State of Palestine." ; Noted that the country's formal announcement will be made at the United Nations General Assembly in September. ; "The urgent priority today is to end the war in Gaza and to bring relief to the civilian population. We need an immediate ceasefire, the release of all hostages, and massive humanitarian aid for the people of Gaza. We must also ensure the demilitarisation of Hamas, secure and rebuild Gaza." ; "And finally, we must build the State of Palestine, guarantee its viability, and ensure that by accepting its demilitarisation and fully recognising Israel, it contributes to the security of all in the region." ; "The French people want peace in the Middle East. It is our responsibility — as French citizens, alongside Israelis, Palestinians, and our European and international partners — to prove that peace is possible." ; Revealed that he had communicated directly with the President of the Palestinian Authority to express his intentions.

a160.speaker: Charles Kushner, US Ambassador to France (post on his official X handle)
a160.speech: Described the move as a blow to peace: "France's decision to recognise a Palestinian state is a gift to Hamas and a blow to peace. I've just arrived, and I'm deeply disappointed. @EmmanuelMacron – I hope to change your mind before September. Free the hostages. Focus on a ceasefire. This is the path to lasting peace."

a160.speaker: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister (post on his official X handle)
a160.speech: "We strongly condemn President Macron's decision to recognise a Palestinian state next to Tel Aviv in the wake of the October 7 massacre. Such a move rewards terror and risks creating another Iranian proxy, just as Gaza became. A Palestinian state in these conditions would be a launch pad to annihilate Israel — not to live in peace beside it. Let's be clear: the Palestinians do not seek a state alongside Israel; they seek a state instead of Israel."

a203.speaker: Civil society organisations (CSOs) in Malawi
a203.speech: Say they are yet to mobilise at least K30 billion for voter and civic education to avert possible voter apathy ahead of the September 16 General Election.

a203.speaker: Benedicto Kondowe, chairperson of the Civil Society Elections Integrity Forum
a203.speech: Said the lack of funding is standing in the way of CSOs’ efforts to support the Malawi Electoral Commission (MEC) in the voter and civic education exercises. “CSOs need at least K30 billion for the exercise. We call on development partners to support CSOs with resources.” ; Said ensuring that those who have registered turn up on polling day is key to promoting democracy in Malawi, hence the need for intensified awareness campaigns ; Observed that most donors who have been supporting CSOs with funding have over the years reduced or withdrawn their assistance, a development that has affected the capacity of CSOs accredited to conduct civic and voter education: “Many accredited NGOs and other civic actors do not have funding for these crucial programmes, leaving millions of voters uninformed on the importance of participating in elections. If this challenge is not urgently addressed, we risk an even lower voter turnout on polling day.” ; Called on CSOs to also mainstream civic and voter education into other programmes that they carry out.

a203.speaker: Moses Mkandawire, Nyika Institute director and international elections observer
a203.speech: Agreed that NGOs are facing funding challenges which are affecting civic and voter education efforts. He feared that the freezing of United States Agency for International Development (USAid) funding could worsen the situation and appealed to other development partners to come in and support the CSOs with resources ; “If we don’t address the governance issues, there is no way you can claim that you will succeed in running projects in other sectors like education, health and agriculture. How do you do that when the whole governance system has been distorted? There is no accountability mechanism.” ; Called on government to provide adequate resources to MEC so that the electoral body can subcontract CSOs to undertake the civic and voter education exercise ; “All stakeholders should take part in motivating Malawians to vote. There is a need to ensure that responsibilities are being adhered to, and are being promoted at all levels so that we have clean, credible, legitimate as well as free and fair elections. Politicians should also desist from campaigns that will frustrate voters.”

a203.speaker: Malawi Electoral Commission (MEC)
a203.speech: Was yet to respond to The Nation’s questionnaire on funding for voter civic education by press time at 8pm.

a203.speaker: Dyson Jangia, United Democratic Front (UDF) spokesperson
a203.speech: Said UDF is concerned that a number of potential voters were left out of the registration process and their right to vote has been affected. “However, the UDF has already started encouraging those that have registered to vote. The change people are looking for will only come if they vote. We need concerted efforts to achieve this. Parties, MEC, government, NGOs, faith leaders, community leaders need to encourage people to vote.”

a203.speaker: Ben Chakhame, People’s Party secretary general
a203.speech: Said the party will see to it that Malawians vote in large numbers despite that a number of people were frustrated by the registration process.

a203.speaker: Felix Njawala, UTM Party spokesperson
a203.speech: Said those that have registered need to be motivated to vote. He said their vote has the power to bail them out from the suffering they are going through. “If people are disappointed with the current state of affairs then they need to vote.”

a203.speaker: Annie Amatullah Maluwa, Aford spokesperson
a203.speech: Also said they will intensify campaigns encouraging people to vote. She said people need to use their vote wisely to change things. “Bad leaders are chosen by people that do not vote.”

a296.speaker: Joyce Msuya, interim chief of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a296.speech: Told the UN Security Council that "acts reminiscent of the gravest international crimes" are being committed in Gaza; described Israel's monthlong ground offensive and ongoing siege of northern Gaza as an "intensified, extreme, and accelerated version of the horrors of the past year" ; said Palestinian civilians had been "forced to witness their family members killed, burned and buried alive" in Gaza, which she described as "a wasteland of rubble" ; "We are witnessing acts reminiscent of the gravest international crimes" ; "The daily cruelty we see in Gaza seems to have no limits" ; "As I brief you, Israeli authorities are blocking humanitarian assistance from entering North Gaza, where fighting continues and around 75 000 people remain with dwindling water and food supplies" ; also called out the indiscriminate destruction of Gaza after more than a year of Israeli attacks.

a296.speaker: International food security experts (report released Friday)
a296.speech: Said the humanitarian situation in Gaza was "extremely grave and rapidly deteriorating" and warned of an imminent famine in parts of the north.

a296.speaker: Danny Danon, Israel's UN Ambassador
a296.speech: Called the reports of possible famine in northern Gaza "baseless and slanderous"; told reporters before the UNSC meeting that the situation in Gaza, including the north, has shown improvement since October.

a296.speaker: Stephane Dujarric, UN spokesperson
a296.speech: Said October saw the lowest amount of humanitarian aid enter Gaza this year, and the war-torn enclave had received "nowhere near what we need to support more than two million Palestinians"; said that for a second month the UN World Food Programme was only able to reach half the people who rely on UN assistance in Gaza, and only with reduced rations; said the other trucks in the aid convoy were unable to make their deliveries because of delays in receiving authorisation from Israeli authorities as well as crowds of desperately hungry people waiting along the route, and that the delivery was the first time in more than a month that people in Beit Hanoon had received any food assistance; said a further WFP mission to Beit Hanoon planned for Tuesday had been denied: "those missions have been denied" ; "We continue to call for the immediate opening of more land routes into Gaza and for the lifting of administrative and physical restrictions within Gaza to efficiently reach the most vulnerable people and areas."

a296.speaker: Riyad Mansour, Palestine's UN envoy
a296.speech: Told the UNSC meeting that Israel has chosen to perpetrate "famine as a method of war" in a process of ethnic cleansing in Gaza ; "Everything we warned against, everything Israel denied, is happening before our eyes" ; "We are at the last stages of an orchestrated plan to empty wide areas of Gaza from its Palestinian population."

a357.speaker: Institute of Human Virology Nigeria (IHVN)
a357.speech: Disclosed that 300 patients died of tuberculosis out of over 6,000 cases recorded in Ogun State in 2023.

a357.speaker: Florinda Olawusi, Senior Programme Officer, Institute of Human Virology Nigeria (IHVN)
a357.speech: Expressed concern over a 100% rise from 2019, adding that 3,000 cases were recorded in 2019, and noted that 95% of patients were already placed on treatment: "Since the inception of TB long 3 project in Ogun state which started in 2019, Ogun state was diagnosing a little over 3,000 cases annually but presently from 2019 till now for example last year in 12 month they were able to diagnose over 6,000 cases which is a huge increment. Its over a 100% increase in the number of cases diagnosed." ; "The treatment lasts for six months. So, what that means is that after six months once the duration of the treatment is complete the patient leaves the program. As at last year, we were able to identify 6,000 cases and 95% of them were placed on treatment." ; responding to questions on the number of deaths: "Yes, there have been some TB related death in the past year, a little over 300 patients died from TB related causes last year in Ogun state."

a357.speaker: Data from the IHVN and USAID TB-LON 3 project for Ogun State
a357.speech: According to the data, 3,000 cases were recorded in 2019.

a357.speaker: Olusola Taiwo, State Programme Manager for TB and Leprosy Control
a357.speech: "One of the predisposing factors for TB infection is staying in over crowded environment, so people should stay where there is good ventilation, indiscriminate pit, they should try put on their coughing etiquette to prevent the spreading of TB germs."

a466.speaker: Scott Bessent, Secretary to the US Treasury
a466.speech: Intimated there would not be any need for further tariffs as these would just put unnecessary stress on the two nations, straining the more, the already precarious ties existing between them.

a466.speaker: Xi Jinping, President of China
a466.speech: Has retaliated in the same measure, vowed to leave no stone unturned, and has directed the shipment of rare earths to the US to stop with immediate effect.

a466.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a466.speech: Hinted at a possible substantial cutdown on China’s export tariffs, according to grapevines and media outlets.

a531.speaker: Those who carry out daily analysis of pharmaceuticals (unnamed drug analysts)
a531.speech: Those who carry out the daily analysis of pharmaceuticals speak of a "worrying situation" that endangers public health, noting that medicines lacking quality may be circulating in the national health system.

a531.speaker: President of the Republic of Mozambique (Head of State)
a531.speech: Wants Sociedade do Noticias and Imprensa Nacional to begin producing the school textbook; the Mozambican Head of State's wish was expressed on Monday, in Marracuene, Maputo Province, in the context of the inauguration of the Maputo International Fair, FACIM.

a531.speaker: National exhibitors at FACIM
a531.speech: See the 57th edition of FACIM as an opportunity for the economic recovery of companies.

a531.speaker: Athletes protesting in Maputo City
a531.speech: Through a demonstration, the sportspeople demand the departure of Kamal Badru from the presidency of the Mozambican Athletics Federation.

a685.speaker: US State Department
a685.speech: Instructed the agencies implementing the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) to immediately resume HIV services, despite the 90-day aid suspension decreed by the US on 1 February.

a685.speaker: Office for HIV and AIDS Prevention of the Assembly of the Republic of Mozambique (report presented to the plenary)
a685.speech: Explains that this is a "limited waiver", with the sole purpose of saving lives, under which HIV treatment services may be resumed, including counselling, HIV testing, prevention and treatment of opportunistic infections (including tuberculosis), laboratory services and management of the medical supply chain ; the waiver also covers prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and pre-exposure prophylaxis for pregnant and breastfeeding women, and PEPFAR funds may also be used for "reasonable administrative costs necessary for the delivery of assistance" ; the "limited waiver" does not cover "activities involving abortion or family planning", or "gender ideology programmes, transgender surgery or other non-life-saving activities".

a685.speaker: Zainaba Andala, President of the Mozambican parliamentary Office for the Prevention and Combat of HIV and AIDS
a685.speech: Said the waiver covers HIV viral load testing "which allows the patient to be monitored to ensure that the medicines used to treat HIV are effective" ; said tuberculosis treatment is covered because "tuberculosis is the leading cause of death among people living with HIV".

a685.speaker: National AIDS Council of Mozambique (CNCS) — latest available data on the HIV epidemic
a685.speech: Show that 12.5 percent of adults over 15 years of age are HIV-positive, with prevalence higher among women (15 percent) than among men of the same age; the most affected group is girls and young women aged 15 to 24, among whom 23,000 new infections were recorded in 2023, three times the number among men of the same age; estimates for 2022 indicate Mozambique had 2.3 million adults and 150,000 children living with HIV; new HIV infections fell from 130,000 in 2019 to 81,000 in 2023 and HIV-related deaths from 49,000 in 2019 to 44,000 in 2023 ; the CNCS believes that over the past two decades 1.7 million new HIV infections and 1.1 million HIV-related deaths have been averted.

a685.speaker: Parliamentary Office for the Prevention and Combat of HIV and AIDS (Mozambique)
a685.speech: Argues that the results "reflect the positive impact of consistent public policies, of the expansion of health service coverage and of the mobilisation of national and international resources".

a969.speaker: Ghana Statistical Service, “The 2022 Demographic and Health Survey” (report)
a969.speech: A survey conducted by the Ghana Statistical Service has shown that over 50 percent of pregnant women in Ghana are anaemic, compared to 40 percent of them who are not pregnant; the report showed that children aged 6-59 months in households were eligible for anaemia testing; it revealed that anaemia prevalence is highest in the Northern region with 69 per cent and 35 per cent in Ahafo; the Survey showed that anaemia prevalence among children had declined from a high of 78 per cent in 2008 ; the Survey revealed that caesarean deliveries were more common in urban areas, representing 27 per cent compared to 15 per cent in rural areas, and said over one in five, representing 21 per cent of live births in the two years preceding the Survey, were delivered through a caesarean operation ; on HIV knowledge, the report revealed that two per cent of women age 15–49 had sex with more than one partner in the 12 months before the Survey, of whom 12 per cent reported using a condom during their last sexual intercourse; the report also showed that 15 percent of men aged 15–49 had sex with more than one partner in the 12 months before the Survey, of whom 18 per cent used a condom during their last sexual intercourse ; the Survey stated it is the 7th report conducted in the country since 1988, designed to provide data for monitoring the population and health situation in the country.

a969.speaker: Dr Chris Opoku Fofie, Deputy Director in Charge of Reproductive and Child Health, Ghana Health Service
a969.speech: said the Survey would provide timely information to the authorities and develop comprehensive policies to address any anomalies in the report; he said anaemia among pregnant women was the major concern because it could lead to increased maternal mortality and poor birth outcomes; he called on the government to invest in health education for the public to be abreast of preventive measures.

a969.speaker: Dr Kyeremeh Atuahene, Director-General, Ghana Aids Commission
a969.speech: urged the government to create an enabling legal policy to address the HIV/AIDS menace.

a1036.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a1036.speech: “Nearly one million people are displaced and require urgent help, especially during this rainy season,” noting that releasing money from the CERF is one of the fastest ways to ensure aid reaches those who need it the most.

a1036.speaker: António Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a1036.speech: said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, new measures to bring unity and reconciliation have spurred great enthusiasm within the country and the enthusiastic support of the international community ; “However, the impact of inter-communal tensions presents a challenge for the new leadership. It is critical to act immediately.”

a1174.speaker: Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
a1174.speech: Warned that the Gaza Strip is the hungriest place on earth and told the press last Friday that the Gaza Strip is the only zone in the world where the entire population is at risk of famine, stressing that the entire population is at risk of famine because of the severe obstacles to humanitarian aid.

a1174.speaker: Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
a1174.speech: Explained that, since the reopening of the Kerem Shalom crossing between Israel and Gaza 10 days ago, almost 900 humanitarian aid trucks have been approved to enter, but fewer than 600 have been unloaded in Gaza ; stressed that an even smaller number of aid consignments has been distributed in the Gaza Strip, citing "congested and unsafe" routes as well as "significant delays" in the approval process ; emphasised that the limited number of trucks arriving in the Gaza Strip amounts to little more than a "trickle".

a1649.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1649.speech: Says the new Land Law, currently under public consultation, opens the way for the elimination of idle land and of the arbitrary allocation of land for mining exploration in the country ; defended the need for a profound revision of land legislation, stressing that "the land belongs to all of us, as Mozambican citizens, and belongs to the Mozambican people," within the framework of strengthening sovereignty and building the country's economic independence.

a1649.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1649.speech: Praised the advances already achieved, namely the approval of the new Land Policy in 2022, and highlighted the forum as "a space for consultation in the process of consolidating the policy and the regulatory framework for access to and use of land," essential to guarantee the sustainable and fair use of natural resources ; "In this sense, the Land Consultation Forum, by constituting itself as a space for consultation in the process of consolidating the policy and regulatory framework for access to land use, seeks to translate, in concrete terms, our commitment to continue making land one of the weapons of our people in asserting our economic independence, whose foundations we are now laying for our Mozambican people."

a1649.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1649.speech: Highlighted the symbolism of the meeting at a time when Mozambique is preparing to celebrate 50 years of National Independence: "The June sun allowed the recovery of the land by the Mozambican people," recalling that land was one of the pillars of the liberation struggle ; greeting peasants, community leaders, women, young people and other actors present, reiterated the importance of inclusion and popular participation in the process of revising the Land Law: "To all of you, thank you very much for your presence at this very inclusive forum."

a1649.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1649.speech: "On this occasion, we want to praise the main achievements of the governance of the mandate that preceded us, which consisted of leading the public consultation process for the revision of the national land policy and the respective legal framework, and the consequent approval of the current land policy and its 2022 implementation strategy, and bringing to debate the present draft Land Law. That is why we are very pleased to see here the former Minister of Land and Environment, Ivete Maibasse, who did an extraordinary job in getting us to this point."

a1649.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1649.speech: "By taking shape as a platform for inclusive debate on issues relating to land administration and management in the country, the Land Consultation Forum allows us to analyse the results achieved on the basis of the national consensuses cemented over some 28 years of implementation of the Land Law in force" ; stressed that it "opens the way for us to adapt and adopt a more robust and predictable Land Law, one that responds to challenges such as the consolidation of market structures, population growth, the increase in the population living in cities and towns without the provision of infrastructure and basic services, combined with the country's vulnerability to the effects of climate change."

a1649.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1649.speech: Detailed the main innovations of the draft Land Law, including the elevation of the Right to Use and Benefit from Land (DUAT) to a basic human and property right, special protection for women, and the prohibition of practices that could result in the emergence of shadowy land markets or the exclusion of local communities ; called for a determined fight against criminal practices associated with land, such as corruption and the illegal sale of plots, stating: "We must, as a nation, eradicate these harmful practices that undermine the development of our communities and of the country."

a1649.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of Mozambique
a1649.speech: Expressed recognition of the Commission for the Revision of the National Land Policy for the breadth and depth of the consultation process, and thanked international partners for their support, such as the World Bank, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the embassies of friendly countries ; encouraged participants to put forward proposals that strengthen gender equity in access to land and help make the new legislation an effective instrument for economic development and social justice: "We also await contributions that clarify the meaning and practical effect of the Right to Use and Benefit from Land within the framework of the market economy."

a1993.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a1993.speech: announced the termination of all trade negotiations with Canada in a post on Truth Social: “The Ronald Reagan Foundation has just announced that Canada has fraudulently used an advertisement, which is FAKE, featuring Ronald Reagan speaking negatively about Tariffs” ; “The ad was for $75,000. They only did this to interfere with the decision of the U.S. Supreme Court, and other courts” ; “Based on their egregious behavior, ALL TRADE NEGOTIATIONS WITH CANADA ARE HEREBY TERMINATED.”

a1993.speaker: Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation & Institute (statement)
a1993.speech: said in a post that a TV advertisement created by the government of Ontario “misrepresents the ‘Presidential Radio Address to the Nation on Free and Fair Trade’ dated April 25, 1987”; stated that Ontario had not received its permission “to use and edit the remarks” of the late U.S. president; added that it was “reviewing legal options in this matter” and invited the public to watch the unedited video of Reagan’s address.

a1993.speaker: Doug Ford, Premier of Ontario
a1993.speech: acknowledged that the advertisement had drawn Trump’s attention: “I heard that the president heard our ad. I’m sure he wasn’t too happy” ; in an earlier post sharing the advertisement link he wrote: “Using every tool we have, we’ll never stop making the case against American tariffs on Canada. The way to prosperity is by working together.”

a1993.speaker: Mark Carney, Canadian Prime Minister
a1993.speech: said Canada would seek to double exports to countries outside the United States due to ongoing tariff threats.

a1993.speaker: Prime Minister’s Office (Canada)
a1993.speech: did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Trump’s decision.

a1993.speaker: Ronald Reagan, late US President (1987 radio address video)
a1993.speech: “Throughout the world, there's a growing realization that the way to prosperity for all nations is rejecting protectionist legislation and promoting fair and free competition.” ; “Now, there are sound historical reasons for this. For those of us who lived through the Great Depression, the memory of the suffering it caused is deep and searing.” ; “And today, many economic analysts and historians argue that high tariff legislation passed back in that period called the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, greatly deepened the depression and prevented economic recovery.” ; “You see, at first, when someone says, let's impose tariffs on foreign imports, it looks like they're doing the patriotic thing by protecting American products and jobs. And sometimes for a short while it works, but only for a short time.” ; “What eventually occurs is, first homegrown industries start relying on government protection in the form of high tariffs. They stop competing and stop making the innovative management and technological changes they need to succeed in world markets.” ; “High tariffs inevitably lead to retaliation by foreign countries and the triggering of fierce trade wars. The result is more and more tariffs, higher and higher trade barriers and less and less competition.” ; “Then the worst happens. Markets shrink and collapse, businesses and industries shut down and millions of people lose their jobs. The memory of all this occurring back in the 30s made me determined when I came to Washington to spare the American people the protectionist legislation that destroys prosperity.” ; “Well, I've never forgotten those jobs and on trade issues by and large, we've done well.”

a2059.speaker: Bayo Onanuga, Nigerian presidential spokesman
a2059.speech: Announced on Wednesday that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has reshuffled his 45-member government, appointing seven new ministers; according to him the President terminated the functions of five ministers and reassigned ten others to new portfolios, and he indicated that the ministers of Education, of Tourism, of Women's Affairs, of Youth Development and the minister delegate for Housing were dismissed.

a2068.speaker: Agricultural Market Information System (SIMA)
a2068.speech: According to SIMA, horticultural markets are showing a general downward trend, even though contrasting variations persist depending on the product; the price falls are mainly explained by a gradual improvement in supply, which now stocks stalls more abundantly and strengthens product availability.

a2068.speaker: SIMA weekly bulletin for week 32 (6-12 August 2025) (document)
a2068.speech: Analysis of the bulletin showed that bananas stand at 904 FCFA/kg (500 FCFA/kg in Maradi, 1,050 FCFA/kg in Dosso); lemons fell 3% to 407 FCFA/kg (down 15% year-on-year); cabbage fell 5% to 369 FCFA/kg (down 21% year-on-year); squash fell 6% to 240 FCFA/kg (up 4% year-on-year); fresh sweet pepper rose 5% to 1,129 FCFA/kg (up 59% year-on-year); potatoes fell 5% to 602 FCFA/kg (down 15% year-on-year); and fresh tomatoes were stable at 845 FCFA/kg (down 6% year-on-year).

a2078.speaker: Education Cannot Wait (ECW), UN global fund for education in emergencies
a2078.speech: According to ECW, of the 222 million children and adolescents affected by protracted crises who urgently need support for education, more than 78 million are not in school at all.

a2078.speaker: Yasmine Sherif, director of Education Cannot Wait
a2078.speech: Declares that the time has come "to stand up for the world's most vulnerable children and young people and to keep our promise by guaranteeing quality education for all by 2030, as provided for by the sustainable development goals."

a2283.speaker: Professor Peter Quartey, Director of the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER)
a2283.speech: Says the recent appreciation of the cedi is the result of a complex mix of domestic and international factors. He emphasised that while the cedi had faced downward pressure, some domestic policies were actively helping to mitigate the decline. He pointed to the government's Gold for Reserves programme as a positive step in cushioning the impact of global economic instability. ; "Domestically, the gold for reserves policy is helping because of what is happening globally."

a2283.speaker: Professor Peter Quartey, Director of the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER)
a2283.speech: Said there were improvements in fiscal discipline, indicating that the government was currently living within its means, spending within the limits of what it raises in revenue. ; "If we were running an excessive deficit, we would have to borrow more, and that would increase interest payments and put pressure on the cedi. But we are not doing that now."

a2283.speaker: Professor Peter Quartey, Director of the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER)
a2283.speech: Commended the improved coordination between the Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Ghana, noting a more unified and transparent approach to economic management. ; "I find the Bank of Ghana to be more engaged now and they are carrying the public along, explaining policies and reforms. When you do that, people gain confidence in the local currency and that strengthens the cedi."

a2283.speaker: Professor Peter Quartey, Director of the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER)
a2283.speech: Pointed to global tensions, particularly the ongoing trade dynamics between the United States and China as a contributing factor to the weakening of the US dollar. However, he expressed optimism that as tariff-related disputes eased and international agreements took shape, global currency markets were likely to stabilise. He urged the government to stay the course with its current domestic strategies, warning that any deviation could reverse the progress made. ; "If we continue doing what we are doing domestically, we will see more stability in the cedi, otherwise, the depreciation could worsen again."

a2283.speaker: Professor Peter Quartey, Director of the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER)
a2283.speech: Called for a more inclusive and balanced policy approach as African countries push towards a cashless economy. He said there was the need for a balanced and inclusive approach that accommodated both cash and digital options, especially for the unbanked, marginalised and less digitally literate segments of societies in Africa's transition toward a cashless economy. ; "Let us not restrict people to only one form of payment. Cash and digital payments should coexist to ensure financial inclusivity and resilience." ; He lauded the theme as highly topical and relevant to today's policy discourse, saying it was very relevant, especially considering the current financial disruptions and the growing push for digital transformation.

a2283.speaker: Professor Peter Quartey, Director of the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER)
a2283.speech: Noted that ISSER, in collaboration with the Innovation for Poverty Action (IPA), was also making significant strides in the digital finance space. "Currently, we are funding about 19 studies through the Gates Foundation across low-and middle-income countries such as India, Ghana, Pakistan and Indonesia. These studies are exploring how commercial solutions and agent networks can be leveraged to reach the last mile," he added. ; "These figures underscore the rising importance of digital payments; however, we must also recognise the persistent challenges in reaching underserved populations, micro and small enterprises, the unbanked, and rural communities," he said.

a2283.speaker: 2024 GSMA report
a2283.speech: Shows continued but albeit slow growth in mobile money usage. According to the report, mobile money users reached 1.7 billion in 2023, marking a 12 per cent increase over the previous year. In addition, agent networks in sub-Saharan Africa have seen 22 percent growth since 2002, now numbering over 18.6 million.

a2349.speaker: United Nations economic report
a2349.speech: According to the recent United Nations economic report, five out of the ten countries the UN forecasted to register fast GDP growth in the year 2012 are African countries, Ethiopia included.

a2349.speaker: Adam Elhiraika, Director of the Macroeconomic Policy Division at the Economic Commission for Africa (ECA)
a2349.speech: Stated that mobilising domestic resources, from both the public and private sectors, is central to Africa's collective success in achieving the 2030 sustainable development goals (SDGs) and the continent's 50-year development plan, Agenda 2063.

a2349.speaker: African Economic Outlook report
a2349.speech: According to a comprehensive look at African resource mobilization by the recent African Economic Outlook report, on average Africa has managed to raise an estimated 441 dollars in taxes per person per year while receiving 41 dollars per person per year in aid, meaning Africa as a whole receives aid that is less than 10 percent of collected taxes; although aid exceeds 10 percent of tax revenue in 34 countries, these countries have shown a progressively higher expansion of their tax base.

a2349.speaker: Roy Culpeper, President of The North-South Institute in Canada
a2349.speech: Stated that in Kenya development is donor-driven, but aid has been useful in building sustainable infrastructure, as a result of which Kenya has been able to build state of the art roads.

a2349.speaker: Government of Uganda
a2349.speech: On different occasions, the government of Uganda stated that in the last few years Uganda's economy has been driven by the growth in telecommunications, the construction industry, as well as the expansion of financial institutions — economic sectors dominated by private investors accounting for about 54 percent of the GDP, as compared to the agricultural sector that accounts for about 24 percent of the GDP.

a2349.speaker: Aniket Bhushan, researcher at The North-South Institute in Canada
a2349.speech: According to Aniket Bhushan, from Africa's 54 countries aid exceeds taxes in only 12 extremely poor countries such as Niger, but under that West African nation's Accelerated Development and Poverty Reduction Strategy (ADPRS), which supports the growth of the private sector, additional revenue from this growth is projected to double the current real GDP growth rate to 11.5 percent.

a2349.speaker: Aniket Bhushan, researcher at The North-South Institute in Canada
a2349.speech: Noted that politically stable and democratic countries in Africa such as Tanzania and Madagascar are now raising alternative resources primarily through increased taxation, trade and domestic borrowing.

a2349.speaker: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)
a2349.speech: According to UNESCO, South Africa, Senegal and Nigeria have the highest number of profit-driven private educational institutions.

a2385.speaker: Elias Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a2385.speech: Called for urgent diplomatic intervention to reopen Goma International Airport and Kavumu Airport in Bukavu, Democratic Republic of Congo, making the appeal during the opening of the virtual extraordinary summit of SADC Heads of State and Government ; stated that reopening the airports is essential to facilitate humanitarian assistance and enable SADC and its structures to find an immediate and effective solution for its mission.

a2385.speaker: Elias Magosi, SADC Executive Secretary
a2385.speech: Described the invasion of DRC territory by M23 and their external supporters, as well as the establishment of de facto authorities and illegitimate parallel administrations in some areas, as serious violations of international law ; noted that these acts demonstrate a clear and unapologetic defiance of both the Nairobi and Luanda Peace processes ; “To this end, collective efforts are ongoing in line with the SADC Mutual Defence Pact of 2003, to protect the people of the region from instability arising from the conflict and to address security challenges in accordance with international law,” Magosi said.

a2394.speaker: USAID Policy Link, Ghana Agricultural Lending Assessment (report)
a2394.speech: Cited as the source for the statement that the regulatory framework constrains innovation because banks are compelled to price loans using the Ghana Reference Rate (GRR), based on policy rates, T-bill rates and interbank market costs, to which they add a risk premium, which drives lending rates upward, particularly in agriculture.

a2394.speaker: AGRA report, ‘Mobilizing agricultural finance’ (cited source)
a2394.speech: Cited as the source for the figure that the agri-SME financing gap in Sub-Saharan Africa is pegged at US $65 billion annually, with agriculture’s wider financing shortfall approaching US $180 billion.

a2520.speaker: Marietou Seck and the other beneficiaries (survivors of gender-based violence)
a2520.speech: For Marietou Seck and the other beneficiaries, it is “a chance to take back control of their lives, to hope for autonomy and social integration.”

a2520.speaker: Guillaume Aguettant, country director of Care Bénin/Togo
a2520.speech: maintains that these women are the embodiment of courage: “Well done for the example you are setting despite the blows life has dealt you… We support you and we will continue to do so,” he pledged ; He presents this pilot project as an example of the pooling of actors working in the social field, indicating that MIHR proves that all aspects (economic, social, legal, etc.) can be taken into account if the actors work together: “The strength of this project is that all the actors work together.”

a2520.speaker: John Bernon, director of USAID's health office
a2520.speech: insists on the objectives of the project: “Getting out of violence is our collective responsibility.” ; He also congratulated the beneficiaries for their commitment, determination and journey, saying the dedication they showed prior to the handover of the kits is the symbol that any victim can find the road to empowerment if the mechanisms put in place to strengthen these women's stability work well, and continued: “The urgent task is to fight against all the violence suffered by girls and women throughout Benin.”

a2520.speaker: Rolande Adjovi, representative of the ministry in charge of Social Affairs
a2520.speech: also welcomes the enthusiasm of these women, who are showing the way to others who could benefit from the same advantages.

a2598.speaker: King Letsie III of Lesotho
a2598.speech: Called for the urgent transformation of Lesotho’s natural resources, especially its abundant water, into engines of clean energy and sustainable economic growth, saying the time has come for Lesotho to fully embrace the global shift toward renewable energy; emphasised that it was high time Lesotho exploited the opportunities presented by the global energy transition imperatives, especially those driven by the 2015 Paris Agreement.

a2598.speaker: King Letsie III of Lesotho
a2598.speech: “We are at the turning point in Lesotho’s economic journey” ; “We are now in a transition from the model of exporting labour towards a sustainable economy that is rooted in our own abundant resources, driven by the aspirations and talent of our people, and empowered by new renewable energy. As you have heard, we have launched the His Majesty King Letsie III Just Energy Transition Fund. This is not merely a fund, but a new way of thinking about development . . . it is a privately-led, government-supported model designed to attract both public and private investment to build new electricity generation capacity and unlock energy independence.” ; “Our ambition is to transition from an economy based on the export of labour to one that leverages our water, wind, and solar resources.” He said the fund is aimed at catalysing investment in solar, wind, and hydropower projects, positioning Lesotho as a future energy exporter in the Southern Africa region, and called on all development and investment partners to join and support Lesotho in this historic endeavour.

a2598.speaker: Molise Ramaili, LNDC acting Chief Executive Officer
a2598.speech: Said it was imperative for the corporation to support the HMKL III-JET Fund, as renewable energy has become central to development across the globe: “We cannot leave Lesotho out of this conversation on renewable energy. Renewable energy is part of our strategic plan as LNDC. Again, Lesotho is part of the Paris Agreement and subscribes to the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7, which advocates for affordable and clean energy.”

a2598.speaker: Molise Ramaili, LNDC acting Chief Executive Officer
a2598.speech: Said LNDC has ensured it had a pipeline of investment-ready projects, including those in renewable energy, adding that the corporation is focused on agro-processing: “We believe in agriculture, and agro-processing is a key contributor to growing the economy of our country. We have projects that are already packaged in agro-processing. We are working with our development finance partners in the region because we are part of the SADC Development Finance Resource Centre.”

a2598.speaker: Professor Tshilidzi Marwala, UNU Rector
a2598.speech: Highlighted Lesotho’s remarkable natural endowments for renewable energy generation and underscored the importance of partnerships in helping the nation meet its ambitious development targets; said discussions during the symposium explored opportunities for Japanese public-private partnerships, the role of blended finance in de-risking renewable energy projects, and the role institutions such as UNU can play in bridging research, policy, and investment to advance climate-smart development across Africa.

a2666.speaker: Maria Zakharova, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman
a2666.speech: Summed up the situation: "Kyiv is taking out its impotent rage over tangible military defeats on the civilian population of Russia. The strike on the capital of Tatarstan is also a kind of revenge for the success of the BRICS summit held in October of this year."

a2666.speaker: Maria Zakharova, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman
a2666.speech: Condemned the silence of the West: "We are outraged by the demonstratively hypocritical silence of the 'collective West' and its mass media, which react immediately to any attack by extremists, and especially to terrorist attacks in different parts of the world, but in the present case they act as if nothing is happening with Russia."

a2670.speaker: 40-year-old female vendor injured at the Limpopo Market (anonymous)
a2670.speech: Said the municipal police officers used brute force against her: "They pulled me into the car. They dragged me from here to where the speed bump is. The car did not stop," she recounted in tears, questioning the police action ; "Is this really a country? They say it is to fight poverty, but what poverty are we fighting?"

a2670.speaker: Another female vendor at the Limpopo Market (anonymous)
a2670.speech: Complained that the Municipal Police officers had not deigned to assist the woman who was injured in the knees: "Even now that they have gone, they did not even come back to see this person they injured. Only police come. So we here do not want police, because the police are not to blame." ; spoke of the reasons that led to the protest, stressing that "we are angry, because since we arrived in the morning we have not sold anything."

a2670.speaker: Nelson Pedro, Commander of the Municipal Police of Xai-Xai
a2670.speech: Confirmed the vendor's injury, but claimed there had been resistance during the intervention: "We cannot specify the number. The numbers we have are approximate. We have information that there are more than 1,500 informal vendors, the vendors and other supporters of theirs, who were rioting. We could not remain there with the vehicle." ; said that the officers at the scene were unprotected and that there was a need for an emergency exit to avoid the worst ; "It was during this process of withdrawing the vehicle that one of the women, we did not even notice, hung onto the vehicle, but as the vehicle started moving she ended up falling and was injured, in the situation she is now in."

a2670.speaker: One of the protesters present outside the Municipal Police Command (anonymous)
a2670.speech: "The Municipality must take responsibility, it must bear the consequences. That woman is really in a bad way. The Municipality must see what happened to that woman, then we will accompany her to the hospital."

a2970.speaker: Ralf Wittek, regional representative of the Hanns Seidel Foundation
a2970.speech: Stressed, at the opening of the discussions in Bohicon, that Africa is marked by certain practices that it would be essential to correct.

a2970.speaker: Colonel Placide Ayamou, gendarmerie officer
a2970.speech: Said that community security represents a recent approach to managing the problem of insecurity at the level of the population, going beyond the classic concepts of the fight against insecurity through its actors and its dimensions; that the study of this relatively new concept will have to take into account the principles and strategies that underpin it, the actors it calls upon and its targets; and recalled that community security is perceived as a more suitable response to the feeling of insecurity that grips populations in certain countries, a concept based on prevention and communication with a view to better anticipating the security needs of the population ; Maintained that the concept of community security is such as to reassure the population further and to reduce the feeling of insecurity that grips them, through an approach offering solutions adapted to each specific situation.

a2970.speaker: Simplice Dossou Codjo, Minister of the Interior, Public Security and Religious Affairs of Benin
a2970.speech: Opening the work of the workshop, recalled above all the current security climate at regional and indeed global level, characterised by terrorist acts by Boko Haram and jihadist groups; and agreed with colonel Placide Ayamou that the concept of community security is of a nature to reassure the population further.

a2985.speaker: Experts
a2985.speech: Have highlighted the high cost of smartphones and lack of access to the internet as some of the challenges hindering integration and promotion of digital transmission of extension services to smallholder farmers in Malawi.

a2985.speaker: Dr. Robertson Khataza, Lilongwe University of Agriculture and Natural Resources (LUANAR) lecturer
a2985.speech: Khataza disclosed that farmers are enthusiastic about digital solutions. However, majority of the farmers are not able to buy phones or radios due to limited resources. ; "Embracing digital advisory services is important in complementing traditional face-to-face extension, which can often be limited by logistical challenges. Digital agricultural advisory and marketing services increase knowledge outcomes and in turn increase productivity, market participation, and ensure social inclusion."

a2985.speaker: Dr. Robertson Khataza, Lilongwe University of Agriculture and Natural Resources (LUANAR) lecturer
a2985.speech: Khataza further stated that because of lack of information, sellers/farmers fail to find competitive prices for their produce while buyers cannot find quality produce for sale in their markets. In turn, he said, prompts farmers to sell their produce in thin rural spot markets or travel to peri-urban markets without information about the demand or market price (blind marketing). ; "Farmers incur significant travel costs, and sometimes fail to register substantial sales (spoilage). Buyers/Vendors struggle to find a consistent source of supply: supply fluctuations, low price offers, stockouts and loss of revenue. Productivity and quality challenges can be worse with limited extension support."

a2985.speaker: Chisomo Haswell
a2985.speech: In his presentation, Haswell said ICT platforms are enabling farmers to share knowledge and experiences on multipurpose agroforestry tree species (MPTS) and other agricultural topics. Haswell also stated that modern ICT platforms can enhance and supplement traditional in-person agricultural advisory services, saying this is why the study was conducted to see how ICT-based knowledge transmission can promote the adoption of MPTS among farmers.

a2985.speaker: Matilda Mtambo, Chief Agriculture Officer for Dedza
a2985.speech: Said digital tools have helped extension workers to reach more farmers with advice on various services. Mtambo assured that her office will ensure the platforms are sustained so that more farmers benefit. ; "As you are aware, the government is hit by that high staff turnover, and this has helped us to get in touch with the farmers even when we are far apart. Through digital platforms, the farmers were able to get the right messages for them to continue with agriculture issues in terms of extension."

a3081.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States (cited by EuroNews)
a3081.speech: “We paid 500 million dollars to the World Health Organization (WHO) when I was here and we terminated the contract. They wanted us back so badly. Let’s see what happens”, adding: “it is very sad, though; think about it. China pays 39 million and we pay 500 million, and China is a bigger country.”

a3081.speaker: Alberto Ferreira, Mozambican academic
a3081.speech: “The withdrawal of the United States from the WHO is a form of war, naturally. The rejection of the Paris Agreements is also a form of war. The declaration that he is going to take over the Panama Canal is also another declaration of war.” ; argues that “Trump comes with a whole force, an assertion, of what he perhaps would not have done during five years, during his 45th term. He now wants to conclude with a process of great exclusion.”

a3081.speaker: Alberto Ferreira, Mozambican academic
a3081.speech: Does not consider the United States’ justification plausible: “It starts from the assumption that the United States must rationalise its economy and therefore act in such a way that there are not many expenses. It has another justification, that it has always been the United States spending more than other countries (...) For the entrepreneur, as a trader, which is what Trump is, the most important thing at this moment are not the values of cooperation, not the values of interdependence between nations, not the values of globalisation and of the world context in which the decisions of one influence the lives of all other people (...) it is a rather worrying justification for all the world’s leaders, starting with the United Nations.”

a3109.speaker: Tammy Bruce, State Department spokeswoman (statement)
a3109.speech: Said Rubio had provided waivers for food assistance as well as “some salaries and administrative expenses, including travel for US direct hire staff conducting ongoing programs.” ; “President Trump stated clearly that the United States is no longer going to blindly dole out money with no return for the American people. The secretary is proud to protect America’s investment with a deliberate and judicious review of how we spend foreign assistance dollars overseas.”

a3109.speaker: US State Department (statement of Tuesday evening)
a3109.speech: Did not provide any details about the fate of billions of dollars of assistance to Ukraine, or foreign military financing to other US partners, such as Taiwan. Without providing details, the statement did name some examples of “egregious funding,” including more than $100 million to the International Medical Corps in Gaza, more than $6 million for an “institutional contract for democracy, rights, and governance” in an unspecified location, and just over $600,000 for technical assistance for family planning in Latin America. It also reiterated a carve-out for foreign military financing to close security partners Israel and Egypt.

a3109.speaker: Congressional Research Service (cited)
a3109.speech: According to the Congressional Research Service, the US Agency for International Development, which falls under the State Department, managed more than $40 billion in US assistance in the 2023 fiscal year and employs thousands of staff overseas.

a3109.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a3109.speech: Expressed “deep concern” for the impact the funding pause would have on HIV programs in low- and middle-income countries: “A funding halt for HIV programs can put people living with HIV at immediate increased risk of illness and death and undermine efforts to prevent transmission in communities and countries.” ; “Such measures, if prolonged, could lead to rises in new infections and deaths, reversing decades of progress and potentially taking the world back to the 1980s and 1990s when millions died of HIV every year globally.”

a3189.speaker: Supreme Court of the United States (ruling)
a3189.speech: Authorized a temporary freeze of more than five billion dollars in foreign aid already approved by Congress and covering global humanitarian assistance programs; the decision, taken by the conservative majority, favors the government of Donald Trump, allowing the disbursement of foreign aid funds to be halted while the case proceeds through the lower courts.

a3189.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States (letter dated August 28)
a3189.speech: Told the Speaker of the House that he would not spend 4.9 billion dollars in foreign aid approved by Congress.

a3464.speaker: Don Moynihan, professor at the Ford School of Public Policy, University of Michigan
a3464.speech: Said Americans are witnessing “an extraordinary centralization of power in someone who lacks a top-level security clearance and has not been subject to any Senate confirmation process” ; added: “Musk has unprecedented and centralized control of the basic plumbing of government.”

a3464.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3464.speech: Told reporters on Monday that the billionaire had to seek approval from the White House for any of his actions: “Elon can't do and won't do anything without our approval, and we'll give him the approval, where appropriate; where not appropriate, we won't. But he reports in.”

a3464.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a3464.speech: Has repeatedly said that the federal bureaucracy is bloated and inefficient, and needs to be downsized; he also accuses many federal workers of being liberal ideologues out to thwart his agenda.

a3464.speaker: Employee of the General Services Administration (anonymous)
a3464.speech: Asked who they are more worried about when it comes to the prospect of being fired, said: “Musk. No one is really talking about Trump.”

a3464.speaker: Sources at the Office of Personnel Management (anonymous, told Reuters)
a3464.speech: Told Reuters that at least four current and former Musk aides are part of a team that has taken over OPM, shutting out some senior managers from their own computer systems.

a3464.speaker: Official at the General Services Administration (anonymous)
a3464.speech: Said Musk visited the GSA last Thursday, while members of his team moved into the agency.

a3464.speaker: Michael Linden, senior official at the Office of Management and Budget during the administration of former President Joe Biden
a3464.speech: Said the access by Musk's aides to payment systems gives them extraordinary potential power: “They could get to pick and choose which payments the federal government makes,” Linden said in an interview.

a3464.speaker: Elon Musk and the White House (non-response)
a3464.speech: Neither Musk nor the White House immediately responded to a request for comment.

a3464.speaker: Thomas Moline, former SpaceX senior avionics engineer
a3464.speech: “Those of us who have worked at Elon's companies can see his fingerprints all over what's happening inside the federal government right now. It's a very seat-of-the-pants affair with Elon's loyalists scrambling to execute his every whim and desire as fast as possible.”

a3464.speaker: Governance experts
a3464.speech: Say Musk appears to have already gone beyond the mandate granted by the executive order Trump signed setting up DOGE on Jan. 20.

a3464.speaker: Executive order signed by Trump on Jan. 20 setting up DOGE
a3464.speech: That order mandated DOGE to modernize federal technology and software “to maximize governmental efficiency and productivity”; other orders on hiring freezes and recruitment say DOGE should work with other agencies to make recommendations.

a3464.speaker: Jamie Raskin, US Representative, Democrat from Maryland
a3464.speech: “We don't have a fourth branch of government called Elon Musk,” he told reporters during a protest outside USAID headquarters.

a3464.speaker: Federal employee unions
a3464.speech: Have urged workers not to take the deferred resignation offer, warning it may not be legal, as it is unclear how the payoffs would be funded; unions representing the employees filed a lawsuit on Tuesday to block the administration's plan to offer buyouts.

a3464.speaker: US official (anonymous, told Reuters)
a3464.speech: Told Reuters that more than 20,000 employees were planning on quitting.

a3464.speaker: Nick Bednar, associate professor of law at the University of Minnesota Law School
a3464.speech: Said it was deeply concerning that Musk and his aides have such enormous power over federal personnel and federal payments “when they seemingly have very little accountability”; he said it was also extraordinary that Musk, whose companies have multiple contracts with the U.S. government, had been put in a position that would raise so many questions about conflicts of interest.

a3493.speaker: Bagayoko Aminata Traore, Malian Minister of National Entrepreneurship, Employment and Vocational Training and Chair of the APEJ Board of Directors
a3493.speech: Recalled that, notwithstanding the budgetary context, APEJ has made the search for technical and financial partners its chief battle in order to achieve the expected results.

a3493.speaker: Bagayoko Aminata Traore, Malian Minister of National Entrepreneurship, Employment and Vocational Training
a3493.speech: Said that of the 53 activities planned for the current financial year, 12 have been completed, 22 are under way and 19 are awaiting execution, that is a completion rate of 22.65% against a budget execution rate of 52.38%.

a3493.speaker: Bagayoko Aminata Traore, Malian Minister of National Entrepreneurship, Employment and Vocational Training
a3493.speech: Also announced the recent opening of five new Youth Guidance Centres (EOJ) in the Gao and Kidal regions through the partner PROMAN, bringing the number of these local offices to 13; in addition, the partner has committed to supporting the financing of 175 projects for an amount of 175 million CFA francs, at the rate of 1 million CFA francs per project.

a3493.speaker: Bagayoko Aminata Traore, Chair of the APEJ Board of Directors
a3493.speech: Renewed her thanks to APEJ's partners, notably the services hosting young graduate interns, LuxDev, USAID, SNV, UNDP, IOM, Netherlands Cooperation, the consular chambers and the regional councils, which enable the organization to carry out its mission for the benefit of rural youth and young graduates.

a3552.speaker: Anitah Among, Uganda’s parliamentary speaker
a3552.speech: “The sanctions are gone,” she told parliament, hinting at her expectation of improved ties with the US under Trump.

a3552.speaker: Christopher Isike, professor of African studies and international relations at the University of Pretoria
a3552.speech: “He is a dealer. He transacts based on what he can get.”

a3552.speaker: Christopher Isike, professor of African studies and international relations at the University of Pretoria
a3552.speech: “Trump will use every instrument at his disposal, including AGOA, to strong-arm African governments.”

a3552.speaker: Christopher Isike, professor of African studies and international relations at the University of Pretoria
a3552.speech: Suggested that Trump’s disregard might inadvertently encourage African countries to possibly foster stronger intra-continental trade and deeper relationships with nations in Asia and the Middle East: “If Africa wants to continue on handouts and aid from the US, then it [Trump’s election] is catastrophic. But maybe it is a good thing for Africa so that we can look elsewhere in terms of our trade partners and alliances.”

a3552.speaker: Patrick Bond, professor and political sociologist at the University of Johannesburg
a3552.speech: Said he expected leaders who have faced scrutiny over their human rights records – such as Uganda’s Yoweri Museveni and Rwanda’s Paul Kagame – to try to curry favour with Trump.

a3552.speaker: Patrick Bond, professor and political sociologist at the University of Johannesburg
a3552.speech: Warned that the AGOA could be “up for grabs” as Trump leverages these issues in negotiations.

a3552.speaker: Patrick Bond, professor and political sociologist at the University of Johannesburg
a3552.speech: Emphasised the potential fallout, stating that Trump’s approach would be “catastrophic” for Africa, which disproportionately bears climate change’s consequences despite minimally contributing to global emissions; said that by pulling the US out of climate agreements, Trump would not only curtail Africa’s access to international climate funds – needed to tackle everything from water scarcity to food insecurity – but also embolden polluting industries globally, amplifying Africa’s climate vulnerability.

a3552.speaker: Emmerson Mnangagwa, Zimbabwe’s President
a3552.speech: Praised Trump’s victory, describing him as a leader who “speaks for the people”.

a3552.speaker: Samuel Oyewole, Nigerian political science lecturer
a3552.speech: Remarked that Trump is unlikely to let human rights and democratic norms drive his relationship with African leaders: “The emphasis on human rights and democracy, which was emphasised by Biden, may not be prioritised for strategic interest under Trump.” He warned Trump may actually target countries deemed to be acting against US interests.

a3552.speaker: Samuel Oyewole, Nigerian political science lecturer
a3552.speech: Suggested Trump would also deploy aid strategically, conditioned on the continent’s alignment with his interests: “We cannot consider Trump to be Father Christmas.”

a3552.speaker: Samuel Oyewole, Nigerian political science lecturer
a3552.speech: Pointed out that with Trump’s disregard for multilateral institutions, Africa’s longstanding aspiration for UN Security Council reforms may face new obstacles.

a3552.speaker: Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President (post on X)
a3552.speech: “I look forward to continuing the close and mutually beneficial partnership between our two nations across all domains of our cooperation,” Ramaphosa wrote in his congratulatory message to Trump on X.

a3899.speaker: Madou Sylla, promoter of the Nexten Summit 2025
a3899.speech: “Senegal is facing a difficult period, with 50% of the workforce unemployed or underemployed, 75% of jobs in the informal sector, and an 80% dependency on imports. We're not coming with promises, but with concrete action” ; “Senegal doesn't need more speeches or ill-suited foreign models. It needs to produce, process locally, and embrace a new economic and technological paradigm.”

a3899.speaker: Madou Sylla, promoter of the Nexten Summit 2025
a3899.speech: Said of the NexCF tokenisation platform: “This platform will allow local governments, ministries, hospitals, and schools to raise funds without relying solely on banks or foreign aid.”

a3899.speaker: Madou Sylla, promoter of the Nexten Summit 2025
a3899.speech: “Sixty-five percent of future jobs don't yet exist. This is our opportunity,” highlighting efforts to modernise education, transform agriculture through data and drones, and build a monetised creative economy.

a4417.speaker: Roland Layfette Giddings, Liberian Minister of Public Works
a4417.speech: Said the draft Zoning Act, introduced by the Ministry of Public Works (MPW) through the World Bank-financed Liberia Urban Resilience Project (LURP), is intended to address the numerous challenges and limitations presented by the current Zoning Law of Liberia enacted in 1958; said Liberia had a zoning law which was not really elaborate to deal with some of the contemporary challenges, especially when it comes to urban planning; said the draft law, when ratified by the Legislature, will promote efficient and effective land development and management in Liberia and help to address the many zoning issues presently confronting the country.

a4417.speaker: Roland Layfette Giddings, Liberian Minister of Public Works
a4417.speech: Said urban planning is very key to social and economic development in any country, “if you have to deliver goods and services, if you have to enhance economic growth, if you have to enhance security, if you have to also enhance environmental sustainability” ; “We have to create the kind of coordination collaboration to ensure that this is implemented to enhance the urban planning we need for economic growth and development for our country.”

a4417.speaker: Roland Layfette Giddings, Liberian Minister of Public Works
a4417.speech: Noted further that the project aims to address Liberia’s pressing challenges related to flooding, climate risks, and urban management deficiencies through a US$40 million World Bank endowment ; “The project will invest in climate-resilient infrastructure to reduce flooding, climate risks, and increase access to basic services in Monrovia, in line with the government’s ARREST Agenda, while also enhancing urban management capacities.” ; claimed that the Ministry of Public Works (MPW) is leading the implementation of the project with the support of various government ministries, agencies, and townships.

a4469.speaker: Ville Tavio, Finland’s Minister for Foreign Trade and Development
a4469.speech: Announced that Finland will suspend all humanitarian aid to Somalia, emphasizing that the Somali government’s refusal to repatriate its citizens violates Finland’s expectations regarding international cooperation; highlighted that Finland’s aid policies are based on mutual agreements and the expectation that recipient countries adhere to international standards, including accepting their own citizens when requested.

a4469.speaker: Finnish government
a4469.speech: Said the suspension of humanitarian aid aims to pressure Somalia into complying with repatriation agreements, and that it aligns with Finland’s broader foreign policy, which conditions aid on a country’s willingness to cooperate on migration and other critical international matters ; stated that the suspension will remain in effect until Somalia shows a willingness to accept the return of its nationals and demonstrates commitment to international cooperation standards.

a4597.speaker: Ethiopian federal government
a4597.speech: Has claimed that Ethiopia has become a net wheat exporter despite the bread price nearly doubling in two years.

a4952.speaker: Elsie (pseudonym), community health/aid worker in Msogwaba township, South Africa
a4952.speech: "I was supporting 380 kids, making sure each and every kid is taking his medication, is virally suppressed, each and every kid is not being discriminated or violated," ; "We teach them to accept themselves as they are, to know they are loved. I take them as my own children."

a4952.speaker: Elsie (pseudonym), community health/aid worker in Msogwaba township, South Africa
a4952.speech: Said she fears the worst now that she is unable to visit the children: "My fear is that they won't take their medication"; says some children have gone missing since the programme ended and she is worried that others might miss their hospital appointments: "We know each and every one of those kids and their problems. Some of them won't survive." ; "I was forced to abandon them — they really trusted me."

a4952.speaker: South African government data
a4952.speech: According to government data, South Africa has one of the highest rates of HIV/AIDS in the world, with around 13 percent of the population — or 7.8 million people — living with the virus; in 2023 there were about 640,000 children orphaned by the virus in the country.

a4952.speaker: Government of South Africa
a4952.speech: Has assured the cuts will not affect its rollout of antiretrovirals (ARVs); in February launched a campaign to extend the lifesaving treatment, which already reaches 5.9 million patients, to 1.1 million additional people by the end of the year.

a4952.speaker: Foster Mohale, South African health department spokesperson
a4952.speech: Told AFP: "The country has got capacity to provide… HIV treatment to people living with HIV because almost 90 percent of the current treatment is purchased through the fiscus/government budget."

a4952.speaker: Sibongile Tshabalala-Madhlala, chair of the Treatment Action Campaign
a4952.speech: "It's about much more than medicine. It's about a person finding a friendly healthcare worker at the facility. It's about understanding the challenges of people living with HIV and their needs. It's about prevention, and keeping people in care." ; fears the funding cuts will severely impact human resources in already understaffed and overcrowded hospitals, including by extending waiting periods.

a4952.speaker: Aaron Motsoaledi, South African Health Minister
a4952.speech: Has said the PEPFAR cuts alone meant 15,000 workers lost their jobs.

a4952.speaker: Study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine (February)
a4952.speech: Suggested that cutting all PEPFAR funding to South Africa could lead to more than 600,000 additional HIV-related deaths over the next decade.

a4952.speaker: Sibongile Tshabalala-Madhlala, chair of the Treatment Action Campaign
a4952.speech: Told AFP she believes "people will die": "People won't be able to miss work to get their medication. Some are already sharing ARVs. With this disruption, we will see a rise of infection rates and more HIV-related deaths."

a4952.speaker: Mother of a 17-year-old HIV patient in Msogwaba
a4952.speech: "She helped him a lot whenever he was struggling," sighed his mother, who cannot afford to take time off work to accompany her son: "I feel that we've been abandoned."

a5115.speaker: Bank of Tanzania (BoT) statistics
a5115.speech: Show that in 2024 alone Tanzania spent 147.0 million US dollars (Sh383.2 billion) to import motorcycles from abroad.

a5115.speaker: Land Transport Regulatory Authority (Latra) 2023/2024 report
a5115.speech: Shows a 44.5 per cent increase in bodaboda licences issued in the 2023/2024 financial year compared with the previous year; states the Authority issued 46,146 motorcycle (D1) licences in the reporting period, up from 31,937 in the same period of 2022/2023, accounting for about 54.1 per cent of all licences issued for private passenger vehicles; the largest number of motorcycle licences went to the southern zone (39.1 per cent), followed by the central and lake zones (17.8 per cent each), the eastern zone (16.4 per cent) and the northern zone (8.9 per cent); for bajaji, 22,408 licences were issued, down 12.2 per cent from 25,512, with the southern zone taking 35.9 per cent, the eastern zone 25.8 per cent, the central zone 14.7 per cent, the northern zone 12.9 per cent and the Lake Zone 10.7 per cent.

a5115.speaker: Denis Kaswagula, 2018 college graduate and bodaboda rider
a5115.speech: "There are no jobs; this is the only place I can get a little something to live on, and so far I have two motorcycles after completing the contract on the first one." ; says that after sitting idle for three years since finishing college, he despaired of finding a job, having sent application letters to various places without success ; "I got tired, I gave up. One day, while I was with a friend of mine who is a bodaboda rider, he said his boss was looking for someone to ride a motorcycle, and I thought let me try. I set goals and now life is moving along."

a5115.speaker: Vicent Antony, bodaboda rider
a5115.speech: Explains that through this vehicle he has now bought a plot of land and is continuing to invest little by little so that he can begin building ; "My family is growing; I am looking at how to put up at least a bedroom and a sitting room so we can move in, because I did not get the chance to study, but here I have succeeded a little."

a5115.speaker: Dr Balozi Morwa, economics and business expert
a5115.speech: Said that despite the increase and the jobs it gives to young people, the bodaboda cannot bring them development, because the income is small ; "It cannot bring a revolution; it only keeps them from being idlers. Most of the young people who ride only earn money for food; they have no financial education, they do not know how to save or how to be creative with customers so as to earn income; instead they fall into drinking." ; "Without savings there is no economy; you must save, otherwise know that it is not a life, it is like the life of a bird. Now this makes them continue to cause chaos on the roads and to form their own army and be used at election time because they are easily deceived, so even the leaders who get elected turn out to be unfit, which drags the economy down."

a5115.speaker: Dr Balozi Morwa, economics and business expert
